title: Dealey Plaza
summary: The grassy knoll - the Dallas plaza where President John F. Kennedy was assassinated on November 22, 1963, spawning sixty years of conspiracy theories and endless debate about what really happened.

content.intro: At 12:30 PM on November 22, 1963, President John F. Kennedy's motorcade entered Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas. Seconds later, shots rang out. The President slumped in his seat, his head exploding in a spray of blood. Governor John Connally, seated ahead of him, was wounded. Jackie Kennedy crawled onto the trunk of the moving limousine. Within the hour, President Kennedy was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, he was shot dead on live television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald acted alone, firing three shots from the sixth floor of the Texas School Book Depository. But doubts emerged immediately and have never subsided. The 'grassy knoll,' the 'magic bullet,' the 'second shooter' - Dealey Plaza became the birthplace of modern conspiracy culture, a place where Americans lost faith that their government would tell them the truth.

sections.title: November 22, 1963
sections.body: Kennedy came to Texas to mend political fences. The state's Democratic Party was divided; a successful visit could help secure Texas for the 1964 election. The morning was rainy in San Antonio, but Dallas dawned clear. The motorcade route had been published in newspapers. Kennedy's open limousine turned onto Elm Street and entered Dealey Plaza, passing the Texas School Book Depository. At 12:30 PM, shots were fired - most witnesses heard two or three. The President's head jerked backward; he slumped into Jackie's lap. The limousine accelerated toward Parkland Hospital, four miles away. A priest administered last rites. At 1:00 PM, President Kennedy was pronounced dead.

sections.title: The Suspect
sections.body: Lee Harvey Oswald was a 24-year-old former Marine who had defected to the Soviet Union, returned disillusioned, and drifted between menial jobs. He was employed at the Texas School Book Depository. He owned a mail-order Italian rifle. After the shooting, he fled, killed a Dallas police officer named J.D. Tippit, and was arrested in a movie theater. In custody, Oswald denied killing anyone. 'I'm just a patsy,' he said. On November 24, while being transferred between jails, nightclub owner Jack Ruby stepped from a crowd of journalists and shot Oswald in the stomach. Oswald died that afternoon, taking whatever he knew to his grave.

sections.title: The Questions
sections.body: The Warren Commission, appointed by President Johnson, spent ten months investigating. Its conclusion: Oswald acted alone, firing three shots in approximately eight seconds. One shot missed. One passed through Kennedy's neck and wounded Connally - the 'magic bullet.' One struck Kennedy's head. But critics attacked the findings immediately. Could one bullet cause seven wounds? Why did Kennedy's head jerk backward if shot from behind? Were there shots from the grassy knoll? Later investigations, including the House Select Committee on Assassinations in 1979, found acoustic evidence of a probable second shooter - evidence later disputed. Poll after poll shows most Americans don't believe the official story.

sections.title: The Conspiracy Culture
sections.body: Dealey Plaza launched modern conspiracy thinking. The suspects multiplied: the Mafia, the CIA, anti-Castro Cubans, the military-industrial complex, Lyndon Johnson himself. Oliver Stone's 1991 film 'JFK' presented a vast conspiracy reaching the highest levels of government. Books, documentaries, and theories proliferate. The Sixth Floor Museum contains over 50,000 items related to the assassination. Some details remain classified or disputed. But perhaps the most lasting impact is cultural: after Dealey Plaza, Americans became suspicious of official narratives. Watergate, Iran-Contra, the Iraq War - each scandal reinforced the sense that the government lies. Dealey Plaza is where that suspicion was born.

sections.title: Visiting Dealey Plaza
sections.body: Dealey Plaza is located in downtown Dallas, at the western edge of the city's urban core. The Texas School Book Depository, now the Sixth Floor Museum, chronicles the assassination and its aftermath. The window from which Oswald allegedly fired is preserved behind glass. Visitors can look down at the plaza and imagine those eight seconds. The plaza itself is a National Historic Landmark District, largely unchanged since 1963. Two X marks on Elm Street show where Kennedy was hit. The grassy knoll rises to the right. Conspiracy theorists and tour guides gather daily. The experience is unsettling - a beautiful park forever associated with murder. Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) is 20 miles northwest; Dallas Love Field (DAL) is 7 miles north.

content.flightContext: Located at 32.78°N, 96.81°W in downtown Dallas, Texas, at the western edge of the city's commercial core. From altitude, Dealey Plaza appears as a small green space where three streets converge beneath a triple underpass. The former Texas School Book Depository (now Sixth Floor Museum) is the brick building at the plaza's northeast corner. The grassy knoll is visible to the north.
